extracted.intended_audience: reformers, policymakers, scholars, and educated readers interested in American political and social reform
extracted.subtask_description: A critical, prescriptive analysis of what political, economic, and moral conditions are necessary for the 'Promise of American life' to be fulfilled; aimed at diagnosing contemporary problems and prescribing reforms at the national level. The chapter identifies institutional, regulatory, and cultural changes required to convert a presumed automatic destiny into a deliberate national purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation of existing material and political achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: The better future must bring a continuation of the good things of the past: increasing comfort and economic independence of an ever increasing proportion of the population. 'The substance of the existing achievement must constitute a veritable beginning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any plan to realize the national Promise should preserve and build upon material prosperity, political liberty, and broad natural equality already secured; reforms must not discard these established benefits but use them as the starting point for further progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure moral and social results, not merely material gains
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic and political system 'must be made to secure results of moral and social value'—democracy should become a constructive social ideal, not only a mechanism for material improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and institutions should be evaluated by their ability to produce moral and social amelioration (education, public virtue, equal treatment), not only by growth or rising incomes; the democratic ideal's significance lies in these non-material outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine individual effort with proper political organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing comfort and economic independence must be secured 'by a combination of individual effort and proper political organization.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should preserve incentives for individual initiative while ensuring a political framework that guarantees fair opportunity and guards against abuses that undermine equal access and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the national Promise as a conscious, purposive project
rubrics_metrics.description: The Promise can no longer be assumed to be automatically fulfilled; it must be transformed 'into a closer equivalent of a national purpose, the fulfillment of which is a matter of conscious work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandon optimistic fatalism. Success requires deliberate policy-making, long-term planning, and active civic engagement; evaluate proposals by whether they advance a deliberate national purpose rather than rely on chance or laissez-faire dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate changing economic conditions and institutionalize opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the virgin wilderness and conditions of earlier expansion have changed, 'The same results can no longer be achieved by the same easy methods'—the Promise needs a 'house on a hill-top rather than in a valley.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions and policies that do not depend on frontier expansion or accidental abundance; create structural, durable mechanisms (education, infrastructure, regulatory frameworks) that sustain opportunity under modern conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impose discipline and subordinations of some private desires to national purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Fulfillment 'is to be secured ... not merely by a maximum amount of economic freedom, but by a certain measure of discipline; not merely by the abundant satisfaction of individual desires, but by a large measure of individual subordination and self-denial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept limits on unconstrained private accumulation when it undermines social goals; evaluate reforms by their capacity to balance personal freedom with obligations to the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate to strike at the roots of economic abuses, not merely symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Efficient regulation 'must be regulation which will strike, not at the symptoms of the evil, but at its roots'—targeting the concentration of wealth and power that produces political corruption and unjust institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy design should identify and address structural mechanisms (legal privileges, monopoly power, distorted markets) that produce inequality; avoid superficial fixes that leave the underlying causes intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility for morally and socially desirable distribution of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: In making the state responsible for subordinating the individual to a national purpose, 'the American state will in effect be making itself responsible for a morally and socially desirable distribution of wealth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public institutions should accept responsibility for shaping wealth distribution through taxation, regulation, public goods, and law; evaluate proposals by whether they enable the state to fulfill that distributive role in ways compatible with democratic legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer official national action over voluntary/private remedy for the social problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem 'belongs to the American national democracy, and its solution must be attempted chiefly by means of official national action'—no voluntary association is competent to assume the full responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor national-level policy instruments and legal reforms rather than relying primarily on charity, philanthropy, or voluntary private arrangements when addressing systemic economic and social inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent the perpetuation of advantage by winners
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual competition 'results ... in the attempt to perpetuate the victory' by the strong; this attempt must be 'recognized and forestalled in the interest of the American national purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt measures (antitrust, anti-entrenchment rules, equalizing access) that prevent economic winners from entrenching power in ways that block mobility and democratic equality; evaluate policies for their anti-entrenchment effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit excessive economic freedom where it threatens democratic equality
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional freedom granted to individuals has produced a 'prodigious concentration of wealth' which becomes 'inimical to democracy'; beyond a point that freedom is harmful and 'by way of being fatal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance market liberties with safeguards that preserve democratic processes—use targeted constraints where private economic freedom undermines public equality or political integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use democratic institutions to make social problems inevitable and addressable
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Americans have democratic institutions, 'the social problem is a democratic problem'—inequalities will surface and the people have the power to alter institutions and demand consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage democratic processes (majoritarian politics, legislative reform, civic debate) to surface and solve social grievances; assess reforms by their responsiveness to popular will and capacity to be enacted within democratic frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformers must abandon optimistic fatalism and embrace active civic struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformers cannot believe the future will 'take care of itself'; they must treat redemption of the national Promise as 'a cause for which the good American must fight'—propagated by 'the Word' and 'the Sword' (i.e., advocacy and forceful enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reform strategies by their explicitness of purpose and willingness to mobilize public opinion and enact enforceable changes; rhetorical or purely moral appeals without institutional follow-through are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on systemic causes rather than merely blaming individual elites
rubrics_metrics.description: While those who hold concentrated wealth are not necessarily uniquely immoral, 'the political corruption, the unwise economic organization, and the legal support afforded to certain economic privileges are ... due to the malevolent social influence of individual and incorporated American wealth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and critique should target systemic legal, economic, and institutional supports that facilitate concentration of wealth, rather than merely moral condemnation of individuals; prioritize structural reforms (laws, corporate governance, taxation) that change incentives and constraints.
